### Claude (11-22 04:14)

Not yet. The fix works in a test, but the production model that uses it is still training.

**Shown so far** (model 00t3b: hybrid se_e2_a + se_e3 descriptor, trained on only the ten 300 K hcp/fcc states, 93k steps):
- E(fcc) − E(hcp) on perfect cells is 124.4 meV/atom, against 122.6 from DFT. Model 00 gives 54.
- The per-state energy errors drop to about 5.5 meV/atom rms, from 47 (fcc) and 71 (hcp) in the matching test with the old descriptor.
- Forces also improve: 0.15 and 0.18 eV/Å, against 0.18 and 0.29.

**Not shown yet:** that the same descriptor works on the full data set. That set spans P0–P360 and 300 K up to the high-SIGMA states, and includes vacancies, grain boundaries and the twins. That is the 00h retrain (job 7715007). It has done 26k of 600k steps in 43 min, so it should finish in about 16 h.

When it finishes, the job runs dp test and the per-state error check on all 151 systems. I'll call it fixed if both of these hold:
- the per-state errors are a few meV/atom across all states, temperatures and defect sets, with no hcp/fcc sign split;
- the perfect-cell fcc−hcp difference stays near 123 meV/atom.

**Still to check:** MD speed in LAMMPS with the compressed se_e3 model. Training is about 9× slower than with se_e2_a, so the iteration-01 MD may be slower too.

### Claude (11-22 10:21)

Both runs are on track, but the Green–Kubo run already shows that the MgO dislocation cell itself is the problem, not the dislocation physics.

## Fe DeePMD retrain 00h (job 7715007)
- Training is at 249k of 600k steps after 6.6 h, so it should finish around 19:30 PST today.
- I froze the 250k checkpoint and tested it. On perfect cells it gives E(fcc) − E(hcp) = **123.9 meV/atom**, against 122.6 from DFT; model 00 gave 54.
- The per-state energy-error check on all 151 systems at 250k is still running on the login node. I'll report it when it finishes. The job repeats that check automatically at 600k.

## MgO M1 Green–Kubo run (job 7718928)
It has run 622 of 1000 ps and has about 4 h left. The interim data already explain the nonlinear sweep:

| stress component | slow fluctuation, V⟨δσ²⟩/kT |
|---|---|
| σ_xz (the glide shear) | **1019 ± 14 GPa**, the same in each quarter of the run (988–1060) |
| σ_xy (control) | 10 GPa |
| σ_yz (control) | 1 GPa |

If the two dislocations glided freely, with only the cell's periodic images resisting, this number would equal G_U ≈ 180 GPa. It is 5.6× larger. That means the dipole's own attraction cancels about 82 % of that restoring stiffness, leaving a shallow double well.

**Cause:** our dipole builder (`build_dislocation_dipole.py`) places the edge dipole vertically, with both cores at the same x and no cell tilt. For an edge dipole that is the unstable position; the stable ones are near ±45°.
- A rough estimate for an isolated pair puts the destabilising curvature at about 0.6 of the cell stiffness, close to the 0.82 measured.
- The two wells sit at about ±7 Å of separation. That matches the ±0.015 plastic strain the M1 sweep flipped between.

So the negative G′ and G″ in the sweep came from the cell geometry, not from MgO.

**Fix:** build the edge dipole in the quadrupolar arrangement we already use for the screw: the second core offset by half the cell in x and in z, with the plastic strain carried in a box tilt xz = b/2. That arrangement is stable by symmetry. The check is that the slow σ_xz fluctuation comes out at or below 180 GPa.

The bridgmanite B1 cell was built the same vertical way, so it needs the same fix.

This is in `results_dislocations/M1_edge001_4000K.md` §5 (Eq. 5).

**Decision for you:** should I change the builder and re-run the M1 and B1 pilots (about 15 min each in debug) and then the sweeps? The current Green–Kubo run would then serve only as the record of the broken geometry; I'd let it finish.

<details><summary>result of Bash</summary>

```
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J MgOsweep
#SBATCH --nodes 1
#SBATCH --ntasks 1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 9
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:p100:1
#SBATCH --exclude=hpc-93-36
#SBATCH --partition gpu
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=2GB
#SBATCH --time=1-00:00:00
#SBATCH -o slurm-%A_%a.out
# Generic array job for tools/anelastic_sweep.lammps. Copy into ROOT next to tasks.txt, anelastic_sweep.lammps and
# graph_c.pb; submit from ROOT with  sbatch -J NAME --array=1-N sweep_array.sh  (resubmit unfinished ids the same way:
# restart.mgo is picked up). One line of ROOT/tasks.txt per array task ('#' lines ignored):
#   dir TEMP PERIOD AMP NTOT NCHUNK NAV SEED NEQ MAXCHUNKS MODE TDAMP [DT DUMPN DUMPSTEPS DATA]
# Optional columns default to DT 0.001, DUMPN 0, DUMPSTEPS 0, DATA ROOT/start.data. The task starts from dir/eq.data
# if present (no equilibration); otherwise from DATA with velocities created at TEMP and NEQ steps of NVT.
# DATA may be a LAMMPS restart (*.gk, *.mgo, *.restart); it is converted to dir/start.data once (zero pair style).
# TIMEOUT = time limit - 300 s. The nearest sweep.env (ROOT, up to 3 levels above) is sourced; LMPEXTRA there is appended to the lmp command line
# (e.g. LMPEXTRA="-var MASSES data -var FPARAM kT" for MgSiO3).
source /resnick/home/recohen/.bashrc
shopt -s expand_aliases
module load cuda
conda activate /central/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/anaconda2/deepmd_py311
ulimit -s unlimited
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=9 DP_INTER_OP_PARALLELISM_THREADS=3 DP_INTRA_OP_PARALLELISM_THREADS=3
export EXE=$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/lmp
export LAMMPS_PLUGIN_PATH=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib:$LAMMPS_PLUGIN_PATH
export TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL=0
ROOT=$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
LMPEXTRA=""; for e in $ROOT/sweep.env $ROOT/../sweep.env $ROOT/../../sweep.env $ROOT/../../../sweep.env; do [ -z "$LMPEXTRA" ] && [ -f $e ] && source $e; done
read D TEMP PERIOD AMP NTOT NCHUNK NAV SEED NEQ MAXCHUNKS MODE TDAMP DT DUMPN DUMPSTEPS DATA <<< $(grep -v '^#' $ROOT/tasks.txt | sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p")
DT=${DT:-0.001}; DUMPN=${DUMPN:-0}; DUMPSTEPS=${DUMPSTEPS:-0}; DATA=${DATA:-$ROOT/start.data}
[[ $DATA != /* ]] && DATA=$ROOT/$DATA
mkdir -p $ROOT/$D
cd $ROOT/$D
if [[ $DATA =~ \.(gk|mgo|restart)$ ]]; then
  printf 'read_restart ${RS}\npair_style zero 6.0\npair_coeff * *\nwrite_data ${OUT} nocoeff\n' > restart2data.in
  [ -f start.data ] || mpirun -n 1 $EXE -in restart2data.in -var RS $DATA -var OUT start.data -log none
  DATA=start.data
```

### Claude (11-22 12:50)

I changed the builder, and both rebuilt dislocation pilots are now stable. The MgO sweep is running and the bridgmanite sweep is queued.

**Builder change.** `build_dislocation_dipole.py` now builds edge dipoles in the quadrupolar arrangement by default. The upper core is moved half a cell along the glide direction, and the box tilt is xz = b/2, so that arrangement is stress-free. The old vertical cell is still available with `--edge-geom vertical`, and it reproduces the 11-21 file exactly.

For bridgmanite I placed the moved core b/2 further along (`--quad-dx 0.5`). At the exact half-cell position, a Si–O pair at that core started 0.78 Å apart. With the shift the closest pair is 1.23 Å, the same as in the old cell, and the core settled near half a cell anyway.

**Pilots (minimise + about 40 ps NVT, same model, temperature and settings as before):**

| | MgO vertical | MgO quadrupolar | bridgmanite vertical | bridgmanite quadrupolar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| minimised energy | still falling (σ_xz drifting to −0.5 GPa) | **4.4 eV lower**, converged | — | **20.2 eV lower** |
| core separation along x (Å) | −11.5 to +3.8, flips | **18.5–20.6** (half cell 20.65) | 1.6–4 | **15.3–16.1** (half cell 16.7) |
| mean σ_xz (GPa) | +1.03 | **+0.01** | −2.66 | **+0.34** |

In both quadrupolar cells the dipole stays at half-cell separation, with no flips and almost no mean stress. In MgO the pair still glides together, which carries no strain.

I also checked MgO against the stability test from the Green–Kubo analysis. The slow part of the σ_xz fluctuation comes out at about 110 GPa, below G_U = 180, which means stable. The vertical cell gives about 500 GPa from the same short pilot, and 1019 from the long run. That estimate rests on only 33 thermo samples, so treat it as rough.

**Sweeps:**
- **MgO M1q (job 7817611, tasks 1–4, all running):** periods 0.2, 1, 5 and 20 ps. I lowered the strain amplitude γ₀ to 0.005, because at 0.01 the cores move about 9 Å of the 20 Å to the unstable point. I'm comparing against the existing perfect-crystal runs at γ₀ = 0.01, which are linear. Each task takes about 2 h.
- **Bridgmanite B1q (job 7820552, tasks 1–6, pending):** the same four periods at γ₀ = 0.005, plus a perfect cell at 1 and 20 ps. The dipole's xz shear is the c66 shear, not the c55 of the existing perfect-crystal sweep, so I built a perfect cell in the same orientation as the reference. Each task takes about 1–1.5 h.

When they finish I'll run the lock-in fits to get the change in G* from the perfect crystal. I'll then fit the plan's Debye model (Eq. 3) for the drag coefficient B and restoring stiffness k, and track the cores against the drive phase.

**Other runs:** the Green–Kubo run on the old vertical cell (7718928) is finishing as the record of the unstable geometry. The Fe 00h retrain (7715007) is due around 19:30.

The write-ups are updated in `results_dislocations/M1_edge001_4000K.md` §6, INPROGRESS.md and the run-directory READMEs. The Obsidian refresh found no running Obsidian, so it did nothing.

2. **Key Technical Concepts**

   **DeePMD descriptors and the fcc/hcp error:**
   - se_e2_a carries angles only to ℓ ≤ 1, so it cannot distinguish fcc from hcp. The descriptors differ by 0.4 %, against a 3–5 % thermal spread.
   - The hybrid se_e2_a + se_e3 descriptor fixes it: se_e3 rcut 4.5, rcut_smth 2.0, sel 80, neuron [16,32,64].
   - The small se_e3 [2,4,8] and DPA-1 did not help.
   - se_e3 trains about 9× slower: 0.075 against 0.0085 s/batch on a P100.

   **The energy errors (not offsets):** they are structure-, volume- and T-dependent. Model 00:
   - hcp +35..+87 and fcc −30..−55 meV/atom at 300 K;
   - fcc−hcp = 54 meV/atom against DFT 122.6;
   - this affects SF, twin and partial energies, the E–P consistency and free energies.

   **Dislocation dipole physics:**
   - Vertical edge dipole (both cores at the same x, no tilt) = the unstable configuration; the stable ones are near 45°.
   - In the M1 cell this gives a double well at ±7 Å. The sweep flipped between the wells, giving nonlinear and unphysical G′/G″.
   - Quadrupolar arrangement: upper core glided by Lx/2, tilt xz = b/2 (Bulatov & Cai §5.5) = a stable symmetric minimum.

   **Stability criterion (results doc Eq. 5):**
   - Free glide gives V⟨δσ²⟩/kT = G_U.
   - V⟨δσ²⟩/kT = G_U/(1 − κ_d/κ_im) in general.
   - Vertical M1 GK gives 1019 GPa, so κ_d/κ_im ≈ 0.82.

   **Solid GK formula (results doc Eqs. 3–4):**
   - G*(ω) = G_B − (V/kT)[C(0) − iω∫C e^{−iωt}dt].
   - Slow part: ΔG = V·C_slow(0)/kT with τ.

   **Plan equations:** Eq. 3 is the Debye form, τ = B/(k + ρb²G_U). With k ≈ 0 (Maxwell), G′/G″ = ωτ.

```
#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Lock-in analysis of oscillatory-deformation MD (LAMMPS fix deform wiggle).

Fits stress and strain to  a + b t + sum_k [s_k sin(k w t) + c_k cos(k w t)]
at the KNOWN drive angular frequency w = 2 pi / period, k = 1..nharm.
Complex amplitudes at k=1 give the complex modulus
    M* = sigma_1 / eps_1 = M' + i M''      (Eq. 1)
    tan(delta) = M'' / M'                  (Eq. 2)
    eta'(w)    = M'' / w                   (Eq. 3)
Shear (xz): M* = G*.  Uniaxial (x): M* = K* + 4/3 G*  and M''/w = zeta + 4/3 eta.

Stress sign: sigma = -P_ab (LAMMPS pressure tensor), bar -> Pa (x1e5).
Error bars: the series is cut into nblock blocks of whole cycles and each block
is fit independently; std/sqrt(nblock) is reported.
Nonlinearity: |sigma_2|/|sigma_1| and |sigma_3|/|sigma_1| are printed.

Input: whitespace columns with a header line naming columns, e.g. the output of
extract_thermo.sh (Step ... Pxz ... Xz) or a fix ave/time file
(# TimeStep v_pxz v_xz v_lz).  Column names are matched case-insensitively
after stripping 'v_', 'c_', 'f_' prefixes.

Usage:
  anelastic_lockin.py FILE --period PS [--mode shear|uniaxial] [--dt 0.001] [--cols a,b,..]
                      [--L0 Å] [--skip-cycles 2] [--nblock 5] [--nharm 3]
"""


def read_table(fname, cols=None):
    header = None
    rows = []
    with open(fname) as f:
        for line in f:
            s = line.strip()
            if not s:
                continue
            toks = s.lstrip('#').split()

**Tool `Bash`** — Compute final Green–Kubo stress-fluctuation numbers

```
source ~/cohen_env/bin/activate; cd /groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/LAMMPS/MgO/4096atoms/V6.6868/4096atom/Dislocations/M1_edge001_4000K_GK; tail -2 slurm-7718928.out; python - <<'EOF'
import numpy as np
d=np.loadtxt('pres.dat',comments='#'); print(d.shape, d[0,0], d[-1,0])
st=d[:,0]; ok=np.r_[True,np.diff(st)>0]; d=d[ok]
H=open('eq.data').read().split('\n')
import re
L={}
for l in H[:30]:
    for k in ('xlo','ylo','zlo'):
        if k+' ' in l: a,b=map(float,l.split()[:2]); L[k]=b-a
V=L['xlo']*L['ylo']*L['zlo']*1e-30; kT=1.380649e-23*4000
for j,n in ((5,'xz'),(4,'xy'),(6,'yz')):
    s=d[:,j]*1e5; ns=len(s)//500*500; b=s[:ns].reshape(-1,500).mean(1)  # 500 samples*2 steps = 1 ps
    q=[np.var(x)*V/kT/1e9 for x in np.array_split(b,4)]
    print(n, 'rms GPa %.2f'%(s.std()/1e9), 'full V<ds2>/kT %.0f'%(np.var(s)*V/kT/1e9), '1ps-avg %.0f'%(np.var(b)*V/kT/1e9), 'quarters', ['%.0f'%x for x in q])
print('ps', (d[-1,0]-d[0,0])/1000)
EOF

### Claude (11-22 16:10)

I wrote the restart: `ANELASTICITY_RESTART_2026-11-22.md`. Before writing it I checked the queue: all the dislocation jobs had finished, so I ran the lock-in fits and the final Green–Kubo numbers to make the restart accurate. Tracking the cores against the drive phase and fitting the plan's Eq. 3 are still to do.

**What the restart covers:**
- 11-20 and 11-21, briefly, since no restart was written on those days.
- The Fe energy-error fix. The old descriptor can't tell fcc from hcp, and adding a three-body (se_e3) term fixes it.
- The 00h retrain: at step 479k of 600k at 16:10, due to finish around 19:30.
- The dislocation work: why the vertical dipole was unstable, the builder change, the pilots, and the sweep results.
- Jobs, run directories, changed tools and next-session priorities.

**Green–Kubo, final (1 ns on the old vertical cell):** the slow σ_xz fluctuation term V⟨δσ²⟩/kT is 1011 GPa (quarters 912–1058). The 622 ps interim was 1019, so it is unchanged and still confirms the vertical cell is unstable.

**Lock-in fits (γ₀ = 0.005), G′ / G″ in GPa:**

| period | MgO dipole | MgO perfect | bridgmanite dipole | bridgmanite perfect (c66) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 ps | 165.5 / 19.0 | 180.6 / −5.0 | 308.4 / −2.2 | not run |
| 1 ps | **312.7 / −97.2** | 179.8 / −0.7 | 200.8 / 12.3 | 259.4 / 4.4 |
| 5 ps | 88.9 / 12.6 (nonlinear, \|σ₃/σ₁\| 0.15) | 179.0 / 0.2 | 220.7 / −0.5 | — |
| 20 ps | 82.5 / 8.1 | 179.4 / −0.9 | 221.7 / 4.7 | 256.4 / 0.5 |

- **Bridgmanite:** the response is linear (\|σ₃/σ₁\| ≤ 0.014). At 5–20 ps the dipole lowers G′ by about 35 GPa and adds no loss, so it relaxes in about 1 ps or less. The 1 ps point softens more (ΔG′ = −59) than the slower ones, which is odd and needs checking.
- **MgO:** the 1 ps point still has G″ < 0, which a linear passive response cannot give. The old vertical cell did the same at 1 ps (238 / −195), so the quadrupolar rebuild did not remove it. The perfect cell at 1 ps is normal, so the lock-in analysis itself is not at fault. The 0.2 ps and 20 ps points look physical.
- **First task next session:** look at the MgO 1 ps run: the stress and strain time series, whether the cores lock to the drive, and the thermostat energy.

I added the final Green–Kubo numbers and a new §7 with this table to `results_dislocations/M1_edge001_4000K.md`, and updated INPROGRESS.md and the ANELASTICITY_TODO.md log. The Obsidian refresh found no running Obsidian, so it did nothing.

import numpy as np, sys
d=sys.argv[1]; P=float(sys.argv[2]); W=int(sys.argv[3])  # window in cycles
s=np.loadtxt(d+'/stress.dat',comments='#'); e=np.loadtxt(d+'/strain.dat',comments='#')
def uniq(a):
    _,i=np.unique(a[:,0][::-1],return_index=True); return a[::-1][i]
s=uniq(s); e=uniq(e); st=np.intersect1d(s[:,0],e[:,0])
s=s[np.isin(s[:,0],st)]; e=e[np.isin(e[:,0],st)]
t=st*0.001; w=2*np.pi/P
sig=-s[:,1]*1e-4  # GPa
gam=(e[:,1]-e[0,1])/e[:,3]
def fit(t,y,nh=3):
    A=[np.ones_like(t),t-t.mean()]
    for k in range(1,nh+1): A+= [np.sin(k*w*t),np.cos(k*w*t)]
    A=np.array(A).T; c=np.linalg.lstsq(A,y,rcond=None)[0]; return c
print('# t0 t1 (ps)  G\' G\'\' (GPa)  mean sigma  |s2/s1| |s3/s1|  mean T  mean PE')
n=int(round(P*W/(t[1]-t[0])))
for i in range(0,len(t)-n+1,n):

**Tool `Bash`** — Extract drive-frequency n=1 mode amplitude per block

```
cd /resnick/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/tmp/claude-25175/-resnick-home-recohen-Claude-Anelasticity/b662d795-e17c-4f1f-98bf-5406b2fd0e6d/scratchpad; source ~/cohen_env/bin/activate; python - <<'EOF'
import numpy as np
for p in (1,5,20):
    d=np.loadtxt(f'zmode_P{p}.txt'); t=d[:,0]; A=d[:,3]+1j*d[:,4]; w=2*np.pi/p
    print(f'== P{p}: drive-frequency component of A1 (complex amplitude of e^(i w t), A), in 20-ps blocks')
    out=[]
    for t0 in range(0,200,20):
        m=(t>=t0)&(t<t0+20)
        X=np.c_[np.ones(m.sum()),t[m]-t[m].mean(),np.cos(w*t[m]),np.sin(w*t[m])]
        cr=np.linalg.lstsq(X,A[m].real,rcond=None)[0]; ci=np.linalg.lstsq(X,A[m].imag,rcond=None)[0]
        amp=np.sqrt(cr[2]**2+cr[3]**2+ci[2]**2+ci[3]**2)
        out.append(f'{t0:3d}:{amp:5.2f}')
    print('  '.join(out))
d=np.loadtxt('zmode_P1.txt'); t=d[:,0]; im=d[:,4]; k=np.round(t/0.5).astype(int); alt=im*(-1)**(k+1)
print('P1 alternating Im A1 (A), 5-ps means:', ' '.join('%.2f'%alt[(t>=a)&(t<a+5)].mean() for a in range(0,200,5)))
EOF
```

### Claude (11-22 16:23)

The 1 ps anomaly is not dislocation physics. It is a resonance between the 1 ps drive and a sound wave that fits exactly into the 60 Å cell. A test run of the fix I propose is in the debug queue.

**What gives it away.** In the 1 ps run the atoms carry a standing shear wave that the drive does not impose. It is a sine wave along z, one wavelength per cell, oscillating at the drive frequency. It grows to about 1.6 Å within about 5 ps and then stays there. The 5 ps and 20 ps runs show almost none of it (about 0.07 Å). I measured it from the dumped atomic positions after removing the box deformation.

**Why 1 ps.** The slowest shear wave this cell can hold has a frequency of shear-wave speed / Lz. With the measured perfect-crystal G′ of 179 GPa and the density of 5.00 g/cm³, that speed is 5.99 km/s. So:

- **MgO dipole cells (old vertical and new quadrupolar, Lz = 60.29 Å):** 0.993 THz, a period of 1.007 ps. That sits right on the 1 ps drive. The old vertical cell had the same Lz, which is why it showed the same 1 ps anomaly (238 / −195 GPa).
- **Perfect MgO reference (Lz = 30.14 Å):** 1.99 THz, so its 1 ps run is far from resonance and normal.
- **Bridgmanite B1q cell (Lz = 36.79 Å):** about 1.9 THz. At 1 ps it is about halfway to resonance. That may explain why its 1 ps point softens more than its 5 and 20 ps points, but I haven't tested this.

**Why the drive excites the wave.** The sweeps shear the box with LAMMPS `fix deform … remap v` plus the `nvt/sllod` thermostat. In that scheme the atoms' flow velocity is not sped up or slowed down as the shear rate oscillates. The missing momentum enters only where atoms cross the top/bottom (z) cell boundary. That leaves a sawtooth-shaped velocity error across the cell, and its longest-wavelength part has exactly the measured shape: zero at z = 0 and Lz/2, maximum at Lz/4 and 3Lz/4. On resonance it builds up to about 17× the error itself.

**Why G″ < 0, the potential-energy rise and the pressure drop.**
- **Stress:** in a perfect crystal such a wave averages out of the cell stress, which is why the perfect 1 ps run looks normal. In the dipole cell the dislocations sit at the wave's displacement maxima and respond to it. That changes the average stress.
- **Sign of G″:** the energy feeding the wave enters through the boundary velocity correction, not through the work the box does on the crystal. So the box-work accounting can go negative.
- **Potential energy and pressure:** the thermostat treats the wave's motion as heat, so the atoms' true thermal temperature drops. That shows up as the potential energy running 23–37 eV above the 5 and 20 ps runs and the pressure about 2–4 GPa low. The old vertical cell at 1 ps shows the same signs.

**Fix.** I added an option `REMAP x` to `tools/anelastic_sweep.lammps`: the atom positions move with the box every step, and an ordinary thermostat acts on the full velocities. The default (`v`) is unchanged, so earlier runs are unaffected. Job 7848423 (debug, `Dislocations/M1q_remapx_test`) reruns the 1 ps dipole case for 30 ps from the same starting state. If the diagnosis is right, the wave disappears, G″ becomes ≥ 0 and the potential energy stays flat. I'll analyse it as soon as it finishes.

**What this means for the existing results:**
- MgO 5 and 20 ps are clean: no wave.
- The 0.2 ps points may also be affected: they lie near the dipole cell's fifth harmonic (about 4.8 THz). The perfect MgO run at 0.2 ps already had G″ = −5.0 ± 0.1 and a potential energy 63 eV low.
- Bridgmanite 1 ps may carry a milder off-resonance version.
- If `remap x` works, I'd rerun the 0.2 and 1 ps points of both systems, and their perfect references, with it.

### Claude (11-22 16:45)

The remap-x test confirms the diagnosis. With the corrected drive the standing wave is gone and G″ is positive, but its size needs one more check, which is running now.

**Result (job 7848423, 30 ps, same starting state and drive as the original 1 ps run):**

| | old drive (`remap v`), first 30 ps | new drive (`remap x`) |
|---|---|---|
| sin(2πz/Lz) wave amplitude | 0.6–1.8 Å | 0.01–0.19 Å |
| potential energy (eV) | rises from −18354 to −18322 | flat at −18359 (the 5 and 20 ps runs sit at −18354) |
| G″ | changes sign between 5 ps windows | **+135 ± 10 GPa** in every window (107 to 172) |
| G′ | 207–520 GPa | 146 ± 9 GPa |
| \|σ₃/σ₁\| (nonlinearity) | 0.04–0.10 | 0.02 (linear) |

So the anomaly comes from how the sweep drives the shear. The old option lets the 1 ps drive build up a standing shear wave across the 60 Å cell. It is not a property of the dislocations, and the quadrupolar rebuild was never going to fix it.

**Open question: is G″ = 135 GPa real?** A simple relaxation can produce at most half the total softening as loss. The 20 ps run gives a softening of about 97 GPa, so the ceiling is about 48 GPa, and 135 is well above it. A loss that large needs either a resonance or an artefact of the new drive.

A resonance is plausible. The two dislocations can oscillate against each other, with the cell itself acting as the spring. A rough estimate gives that oscillation about 0.7 THz, with a quality factor of about 1.4 if I use B = 1.76 × 10⁻⁴ Pa s. That would sit close to the 1 ps drive. These are order-of-magnitude numbers, not a fit. If it is real, it is an oscillation set by the cell size and does not carry over to the Earth.

**Running now:** job 7850736 (debug, about 15 min) drives the perfect MgO crystal at 1 ps with the new option. If it gives G′ ≈ 180 and G″ ≈ 0, the 135 GPa is the dislocations' real response in this cell; otherwise the new option has its own artefact.

**What this means for the existing results:**
- MgO 5 and 20 ps are unaffected (no wave).
- The 0.2 ps points are in doubt for both the dipole and the perfect cell. The dipole cell has a nearby wave mode at about 4.8 THz, and the perfect MgO run at 0.2 ps already showed G″ = −5.0 GPa and a potential energy 63 eV low.
- Bridgmanite's 1 ps point may carry a milder version, since its cell's lowest mode is at about 1.9 THz.
- If the control passes, I'll rerun 0.2, 1 and 5 ps with the new option for both dipole cells, plus the matching perfect references. For the Debye fit to the plan's Eq. 3, the 5 ps MgO point is nonlinear even with the old option (\|σ₃/σ₁\| = 0.15), possibly because it sits near the dislocation resonance, so I'll lower the strain amplitude there.

The new option is `REMAP x` in `tools/anelastic_sweep.lammps`; the default is unchanged, so earlier runs are unaffected. The write-up is §8 of `results_dislocations/M1_edge001_4000K.md`. The test directory `Dislocations/M1q_remapx_test` has a README.

### Claude (11-22 16:58)

The perfect-crystal check passed, so the 1 ps anomaly is solved: it came from how the sweeps shear the box, not from the dislocations.

**Cause.** The sweeps drive the shear with LAMMPS `fix deform … remap v` plus the `nvt/sllod` thermostat. In that scheme the atoms' flow velocity is not sped up or slowed down as the shear rate oscillates. The missing momentum enters only at the top/bottom cell boundary. This drives the cell's lowest standing shear wave, sin(2πz/Lz). That wave's frequency is the shear-wave speed (5.99 km/s) divided by Lz:
- **MgO dipole cells (old vertical and new quadrupolar, Lz = 60.3 Å):** 0.99 THz, a period of 1.007 ps. The 1 ps drive sits on this resonance, so the wave grew to 1.6 Å, about 17× the size it would have off resonance. That is why both dipole cells failed at 1 ps.
- **Perfect MgO reference (Lz = 30.1 Å):** 2 THz, off resonance, which is why its 1 ps run looked normal.

How this produced the symptoms:
- **G″ < 0:** the energy feeding the wave entered through the boundary velocity correction, not through the work the box does on the crystal.
- **Potential energy 23–37 eV high, pressure 2–4 GPa low:** the thermostat counted the wave's motion as heat, so the real thermal temperature was lower.

**Fix and tests.** I added a `REMAP x` option to `tools/anelastic_sweep.lammps`: the atom positions move with the box every step, and an ordinary thermostat acts on the full velocities. The default (`remap v`) is unchanged, so old runs can still be reproduced.

| 1 ps run | wave amplitude | potential energy | G′ / G″ (GPa) | \|σ₃/σ₁\| |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dipole, old `remap v` | 0.6–1.8 Å | rises from −18354 to −18320 eV | 312.7 / −97.2 | 0.08 |
| dipole, `REMAP x` (job 7848423) | 0.01–0.19 Å | flat at −18359 eV | 146 ± 9 / **+135 ± 10** | 0.02 |
| perfect, `REMAP x` (job 7850736) | — | flat | 179.8 ± 0.9 / −0.7 ± 0.6 | 0.002 |
| perfect, old `remap v` | — | — | 179.8 / −0.7 | — |

The perfect crystal gives the same result with either option, so `REMAP x` adds no error of its own. The dipole's G″ = 135 GPa at 1 ps is therefore its real response in this cell.

**What G″ = 135 GPa means.** A simple relaxation can't produce that much loss. The 20 ps run shows about 97 GPa of total softening, and a single relaxation can turn at most half of that, about 48 GPa, into loss. The likely explanation is that the two dislocations oscillate against each other, with the periodic cell acting as the spring, and that this oscillation is only lightly damped. Rough estimates put it near 0.7 THz with a quality factor of about 1.4, using B = 1.76 × 10⁻⁴ Pa s. These estimates are not a fit. The spring comes from the cell size, so this is not an Earth mechanism; in the Earth the equivalent is pinned dislocation segments, which resonate at MHz–GHz.

**What this means for the existing results:**
- MgO 5 and 20 ps are unaffected: no wave.
- The 0.2 ps points are doubtful in every cell. The dipole cell has another wave mode near 4.8 THz, and the perfect MgO run at 0.2 ps already showed G″ = −5.0 GPa and a potential energy 63 eV low.
- In bridgmanite, the 1 ps point is about halfway to its cell's resonance (about 1.9 THz). Its extra softening may be a weaker form of the same effect.

**Proposed next step.** Rerun 0.2, 1 and 5 ps for both dipole cells, with their perfect references, using `REMAP x`. Use a smaller strain at 5 ps for MgO, where the run is nonlinear (\|σ₃/σ₁\| = 0.15), possibly because it sits near the dislocation oscillation. Then fit the plan's Eq. 3, or a damped-oscillator form, for B and k. That is about 10 P100 runs of roughly 2 h each. Shall I submit them?

The write-up is §8 of `results_dislocations/M1_edge001_4000K.md`. INPROGRESS.md and the README in `Dislocations/M1q_remapx_test` are updated.

# M1qx: M1q rerun with REMAP x (2026-11-22, RC: "Yes submit the remap x reruns")

`~/Claude/Anelasticity/results_dislocations/M1_edge001_4000K.md` §8.

**Setup.**
- Driver: `REMAP x` (sweep.env → LMPEXTRA), i.e. an affine position remap every step plus plain `fix nvt` (TDAMP 0.1 ps).

### Claude (11-22 18:43)

The LAMMPS source confirms the diagnosis. In `src/fix_nvt_sllod.cpp` (lines 115–128 of the 22 Jul 2025 update 2 build), the shear correction to the velocities depends only on the current strain rate. Nothing accelerates the atoms' flow when the strain rate changes, so in an oscillating shear the momentum can enter only where atoms cross the cell boundary. That is what drives the standing wave in the 60 Å MgO cell.

The thermostat's optional `psllod` setting does not add that term either, so it would not have fixed the problem. `remap x` was the right choice, and the 10 reruns (jobs 7854590 and 7854592) are using it.

I added this check to §8 of `results_dislocations/M1_edge001_4000K.md`.

2. **Key Technical Concepts**

   - **Fe DeePMD descriptor fix:** se_e2_a sees angles only to ℓ ≤ 1, so it cannot distinguish fcc from hcp. The hybrid se_e2_a + se_e3 descriptor fixes this: rcut 4.5, rcut_smth 2.0, sel 80, neuron [16,32,64].
   - **Vertical edge dipole:** unstable. The quadrupolar arrangement (glide Lx/2, tilt xz = b/2) is stable.

   - **The 1-ps anomaly mechanism:** in LAMMPS `fix deform remap v` + `nvt/sllod`, the streaming profile is never accelerated when the strain rate changes. Momentum enters through the velocity remap at the periodic z boundary, which leaves a sawtooth peculiar-velocity error.
     - Its n-th Fourier term drives the transverse standing wave with k = 2πn/Lz, at frequency f_n = n·c_s/Lz.
     - c_s = √(179.4 GPa / 5004 kg m⁻³) = 5.99 km/s.

     | cell | Lz (Å) | f1 (THz) |
     |---|---|---|
     | MgO dipole cells | 60.29 | 0.993 (period 1.007 ps), resonant with the 1-ps drive |
     | MgO perfect | 30.14 | 1.99 |
     | B1q (c66 256 GPa, c_s ≈ 7.1 km/s) | 36.79 | ≈ 1.9 |

     - **Mean stress:** the wave averages out of the volume-averaged stress in a homogeneous crystal. In the dipole cell the dislocations respond to it.
     - **G″ < 0:** the energy enters through the remap, not as ∮σ̄dγ.
     - **PE and P:** the thermostat counts the wave's kinetic energy as heat, so the real T is lower, which gives the PE and P shifts.

   - **Source check:** fix_nvt_sllod.cpp (22 Jul 2025 update 2, lines 115–128) does `v ← v·f_η − (dt/2)(ḣh⁻¹)c` and then restores the bias. There is no d(ḣh⁻¹)/dt term, and `psllod yes` would not cure it.

   - **Fix:** `REMAP x`, an affine position remap every step plus a plain fix nvt.

   - **Dipole G″ = 135 GPa at 1 ps (remap x):** this exceeds the Debye maximum of ΔG/2 ≈ 48 GPa (ΔG ≈ 97 from 20 ps). The likely cause is an underdamped relative-glide resonance in the image well:
     - per unit length, k ≈ G_U b²/(LxLz) = 5×10⁸ Pa;
     - m ≈ ρb² ln(R/r0)/4π ≈ 6×10⁻¹⁷ kg/m;
     - with reduced mass m/2, f0 ≈ 0.7 THz;
     - Q = mω0/B ≈ 1.4 for B = 1.76×10⁻⁴ Pa s.
     - This is set by the cell size, so it is not an Earth mechanism; in the Earth the equivalent is Granato–Lücke pinned segments.

   - **The 0.2 ps points are suspect:** the dipole cell's n=5 mode is at ≈ 4.8 THz, and the perfect remap-v run at 0.2 ps gives G″ = −5.0 with a PE 63 eV low. The sllod 0.2-ps PE shift scales roughly as γ₀².

| perfect fcc−hcp | 122.6 meV/atom at V 7.25 |

**Cause: the descriptor.** `se_e2_a` carries angles only to ℓ = 1. The fcc and hcp descriptors differ by 0.4 %, against a 3–5 % thermal spread, so every se_e2_a variant fits fcc−hcp at about 54 meV/atom.

**Fix.** The hybrid `se_e2_a + se_e3` (se_e3: rcut 4.5, rcut_smth 2.0, sel 80, neuron [16,32,64]) gives 124.4 meV/atom (test model 00t3b). The small se_e3 [2,4,8] and DPA-1 did not help. se_e3 costs about 9× in training (0.075 against 0.0085 s/batch on a P100).

**Full retrain `DP/00h` (job 7715007, P100, 36 h limit):**
- input is the 00 input plus the 00t3b descriptor;
- energy prefactor 0.2 → 20, 600k steps;
- data is `00/data` plus the 25 tw13 systems (151 systems).

At 16:10 it was at step 479k of 600k, so it ends about 19:30. Then `job.sh` freezes, compresses, runs `dp test` and runs `dp_state_errors.py graph.pb data` → `offsets.txt` (the name is kept for the running job.sh).

The interim at 250k (`00h/errors_250k_interim.txt`) gives perfect fcc−hcp 123.9 meV/atom. State-mean errors by group:

| group | rms state-mean error (meV/atom) |
|---|---|
| a1_fcc | 6.6 |
| a1_hcp | 5.2 |
| vac | 6.7 |
| vacmig | 7.8 |
| s7 | 4.2 |
| s7slide | 4.4 |
| tw13 | 4.6 |
| tw13slide | 4.9 |
| old | 3.0 |
| old_b | 2.2 |
| all states at SIGMA < 0.07 | 4.7 (model 00: 27.6) |

Forces are 0.14–0.23 eV/Å.

**Tools:**
- `tools/dp_state_errors.py`: the old name `dp_state_offsets.py` is a symlink. It evaluates 2 frames at a time, because se_e3 exhausted login-node memory.
- Scratch `pe.py` evaluates perfect fcc/hcp.

**Next for Fe:**
1. Check `00h/offsets.txt`, `dptest.log`, and the perfect fcc−hcp with the final graph.

# Fe DeePMD model 00: the structure- and volume-dependent energy errors and their fix (2026-11-21/22)

Run dirs: `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/VASP/Fe/hcp_fcc/ML/DP/{00,00e,00f,00t,00tnv,00tE,00tEF,00t3,00ta,00t3b,00h}`,
DFT checks in `.../ML/R1/{eostest,phasetest}`. Tool: `tools/dp_state_errors.py`.

## 1. Symptom

Not an offset: a constant shift would be harmless, but these change sign between hcp and fcc and grow with compression
(RC 11-22: "A shift that depends on volume and structure is not an offset"); they are energy errors in $E(V,\text{structure},T)$.

Model 00 (se_e2_a, rcut 6, 600k steps, 623 frames) fits forces to 0.15–0.34 eV/Å, but each thermodynamic state has its
own mean energy error

$$\Delta_s=\big\langle (E_{DP}-E_{DFT})/N\big\rangle_{s} \tag{1}$$

of +35 to +87 meV/atom for hcp and −30 to −55 meV/atom for fcc at 300 K, with a within-state scatter of only 1–4 meV/atom.
The errors depend on structure (sign), volume and SIGMA: they shrink with SIGMA and are ~0 at SIGMA ≥ 0.3 eV. On perfect cells at $V = 7.25$ Å³/atom, model 00 gives
$E_{fcc}-E_{hcp} = 54$ meV/atom.

## 2. The DFT labels are consistent

RC asked whether two kinds of energy were mixed (enthalpy against energy). They were not: every label is TOTEN, read by
dpdata vasp/outcar. PV would be about 5 eV/atom with the same sign for both phases, and $E_{TOTEN}-E(\sigma\to0)$ is −1
meV/atom at 300 K. Direct checks:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| energy vs stress: $-\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}V$ from $V\times0.99, 1.01$ against the Simpson mean of $P$ (eostest, hcp/fcc P100/P200) | difference 1.10–1.23 GPa, the same for all four states (Pulay-like, uniform) |
| energy vs force: the largest-force atom displaced ±0.01 Å along $F$ (eostest `_fm`, `_fp`) | $-\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}s$ = 3.7593 against $F\cdot\hat u$ = 3.7590 eV/Å (hcp), 3.5020 against 3.5010 (fcc) |
| k-mesh: 64-atom cell, 4-point shifted mesh, against primitive cells at 24³ (phasetest) | 3–6 meV/atom |
| perfect-crystal phase difference at $V=7.25$, $c/a=1.60$ | $E_{fcc}-E_{hcp}$ = 122.8 (primitive), 122.6 (64-atom MP 4³), 128.4 meV/atom (64-atom shifted 4-point) |

## 3. Cause: the descriptor cannot tell fcc from hcp

The se_e2_a descriptor is built from the generalized coordinates $s(r)\,(1,\hat{\mathbf r})$:

$$\mathcal D_{mn}=\sum_{j,k} g_m(r_{ij})\,g_n(r_{ik})\,s(r_{ij})\,s(r_{ik})\,\big(1+\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij}\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}_{ik}\big) \tag{2}$$

ANELASTICITY_TODO.md:78:- **11-16:** A3 analysed: O vacancy fast (0.9–1.9 eV), V_Mg slow (4.7–6.0 eV); bridgmanite formation energies need a hop-proof method (proposal INPROGRESS §3, ≈ 60 P100-h). MgO TST confirmed (κ ≈ 1). Σ5 locked at 90/120 GPa up to 3400/3800 K.

# DP/00h: model 00 with the hybrid se_e2_a + se_e3 descriptor (2026-11-22)
Model 00 (se_e2_a only) had per-state energy offsets, hcp +35..+87 and fcc -30..-55 meV/atom at 300 K, and gave
E(fcc) - E(hcp) = 54 meV/atom on perfect cells at V = 7.25 A^3/atom against DFT 122.6 (R1/phasetest). The DFT labels
are self-consistent (E vs P, E vs F, k-mesh; see INPROGRESS). The cause is the descriptor: se_e2_a carries angles only
to l = 1, which vanish at fcc and hcp sites, so the two phases differ by 0.4 % in the descriptor against a 3-5 %
thermal spread. Descriptor tests on the 300 K states only (00t, 00tnv, 00tE, 00tEF, 00t3, 00ta): all near 0 meV/atom.
00t3b (se_e2_a + se_e3 rcut 4.5, rcut_smth 2.0, sel 80, neuron [16,32,64]) gives 124.4 meV/atom and state offsets
of rms 5.5 meV/atom (00t: 47-71).
Here: the same input as 00 (all ../00/data, 600k steps, lr 1e-3 -> 1e-8 / 3000) with the 00t3b descriptor and energy
weight 0.2 -> 20 (00: 0.04 -> 2). job.sh restarts from the checkpoint if resubmitted.

failed SCF in model 00's collection and were rerun with LREAL Auto / NG 9.6/A / even k, all converged in 70-158 SCF
steps; fe_dp_collect.py --sets def, 8 frames rejected for |F|).

### Claude (11-23 04:18)

The new Fe potential (model 00h) has fixed the fcc/hcp problem, but so far it has only been checked against its own training data. Nothing has been tested on structures the model hasn't seen, so I can't yet say how well it generalizes. Training finished on 11-22 at 19:19 after 15.8 h on a P100.

| | 00h | old model 00 | DFT |
|---|---|---|---|
| E(fcc) − E(hcp), perfect cells at V = 7.25 Å³/atom | **124.5 meV/atom** | 53.8 | 122.6 |
| typical energy error per thermodynamic state (rms), low SIGMA | **4.5 meV/atom** | 27.6 | |
| same, by structure group | 1.7–7.1 meV/atom | 2.9–23.4 | |
| worst single state | +17.7 (fcc, 100 GPa, 2800 K) | +87 | |
| force error (rms) | **0.198 eV/Å** (4.9 % of the typical DFT force) | 0.22–0.34 | |
| stress error (rms) | 0.67 GPa | | |

- **No hcp/fcc split any more.** At 300 K the hcp and fcc state errors now run from −3.5 to +9.8 meV/atom with no sign pattern. Model 00 had hcp +35 to +87 and fcc −30 to −55.
- **Weakest spots.** The hot vacancy states at 300–350 GPa come out about −14 to −16 meV/atom. Iteration 01 should show whether that persists.
- **Speed is the cost.** In LAMMPS on a P100 the compressed model runs 79–103 steps/s for 64–176 atoms, about 5× slower than model 00. Short runs at 300 GPa and 2400 K were stable for the hcp, twin and edge-dislocation-dipole cells. I haven't measured speed for the 4096-atom anelastic cells. If it's too slow there, a smaller three-body descriptor term could be tested, as long as it still gets fcc − hcp right.
- **Not yet checked:** any physical property beyond fcc − hcp. That means the equation of state, elastic constants, vacancy and boundary energies, and melting.

**What I did beyond the summary:**
- **Iteration 01 submitted (job 7906537_1–17).** This is the next step of your loop: our model runs MD, then SOAP+FPS picks frames for DFT. The DFT errors on those frames will be the first test of 00h on data it hasn't seen. It covers 17 systems (hcp, fcc, vacancies, stacking fault, Σ7 boundary, twin, four ⟨a⟩ dislocation dipoles, plus sheared versions) at 25 pressure–temperature states each. Before submitting I ran a 2-minute speed test and raised the time limit to 3 h, since the largest cells need about 1.8 h. I also fixed `fe_dp_explore.py`, which had broken when the dislocation builder switched to the quadrupolar layout on 11-22.
- **Per-state error table regenerated by hand.** The training job's final step failed because it called plain `python`, which isn't the DeePMD environment. The iteration-01 training script already uses the right one.
- **MgO and bridgmanite dislocation reruns (remap x) finished.** I've done only the first-pass fit of the stress response so far; tracking where the dislocation cores went and the resonance fit are still to do.
  - **MgO, 1 ps period:** the large loss survives with the artifact removed. The dislocations add 143 GPa to the loss modulus G″, and the response is linear. That supports the reading that the two dislocations resonate in the cell.
  - **MgO, 5 ps period:** halving the strain did not make it linear. The third-harmonic ratio |σ₃/σ₁| went from 0.15 to 0.21, so the nonlinearity comes from the dislocation motion itself.
  - **Bridgmanite:** linear at every period. The dislocations lower the storage modulus G′ by about 35–40 GPa and add 4–11 GPa of loss from 1 to 20 ps, rising to 28 GPa at 0.2 ps.

## User (11-23 04:34)

The way it's supposed to work is to iterate. So one selects the bad structures by comparing with DFT and redoes DFT on those structures. And the rest of the structures go into the test set. And then one does a selection from the test set, and those become the test structures. And one iterates until nothing changes in terms of the total accuracy.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""SOAP descriptors + farthest-point selection of frames, the equivalent of X. Deng's mldp steps 1-2
(asap gen_desc --fxyz F soap -c 6 -n 6 -l 6 -g 0.44; asap/select_frames.py -n N), written because asaplib 0.0.x in
/central/groups/carnegie_poc/xind/mambaforge fails with the installed dscribe (SOAP(rcut=...) -> TypeError: dscribe
renamed rcut/nmax/lmax to r_cut/n_max/l_max).

Global descriptor of a frame = the average of its atomic SOAP vectors (asap's default 'average' reducer), normalized;
FPS with Euclidean distance, starting from the frame farthest from the mean. Writes the selected 0-based indices in
selection order to OUT (and the descriptors to OUT.desc.npy).

Run with the mambaforge python (dscribe, ase):
  /central/groups/carnegie_poc/xind/mambaforge/bin/python soap_fps.py frames.xyz -n 150 -o fps-n-150.index
2026-11-19.
"""
import argparse

import numpy as np
from ase.io import read
from dscribe.descriptors import SOAP


def fps(X, n):
    d = np.linalg.norm(X - X.mean(0), axis=1)
    sel = [int(np.argmax(d))]
    dmin = np.linalg.norm(X - X[sel[0]], axis=1)
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        k = int(np.argmax(dmin)); sel.append(k)
        dmin = np.minimum(dmin, np.linalg.norm(X - X[k], axis=1))
    return np.array(sel), dmin


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument('fxyz'); ap.add_argument('-n', type=int, default=150); ap.add_argument('-o', required=True)
    ap.add_argument('-c', type=float, default=6.0); ap.add_argument('--nmax', type=int, default=6)
    ap.add_argument('--lmax', type=int, default=6); ap.add_argument('-g', type=float, default=0.44)
    ap.add_argument('-j', type=int, default=1, help='dscribe n_jobs')
    a = ap.parse_args()
    frames = read(a.fxyz, ':')
    species = sorted({s for f in frames for s in f.get_chemical_symbols()})

### Claude (11-23 04:41)

Agreed. The training split already worked that way: the worst 15 % per temperature band go into training and the rest become test frames. Two of your steps were missing, and I've now added both to iteration 01.

**What changed**
- **Test structures (your selection step).** New tool `fe_dp_testset.py` picks 30 % of each system type from the leftover frames by SOAP + FPS. These go to `DP/test/itNN/`. The test set grows each iteration and is never trained on.
- **Stopping rule (your "until nothing changes").** New tool `fe_dp_accuracy.py` scores the previous and the new model on all test structures (energy, force and stress errors) and appends the result to `DP/accuracy.txt`. Before, iteration 01 had per-iteration test frames only and stopped on fixed accuracy targets per temperature band.
  - The loop stops when, on the same test structures, the energy error changes by less than 0.5 meV/atom, the force error by less than 5 % and the stress error by less than 0.1 GPa. These tolerances are my choice; tell me if you want others.
  - The old per-band check is kept as a diagnostic only.
- **Train script updated.** `DP/01/fe_dp_train.sh` and the template in `fe_dp_explore.py` now run split → test-structure selection → retrain → accuracy check. I checked both new tools on a 5-system subset of the 00h training data, scoring models 00 and 00h. The test showed the plumbing works; those frames are training data, so the numbers aren't a real test.

**One problem with the procedure as stated: selection bias.** The test pool is what's left after the previous model's worst frames go to training, so the newest test set flatters the previous model. From iteration 02 on, the stopping rule therefore uses only the earlier iterations' test sets, which the newer models never chose from. In iteration 01 only one test set exists, so the 00h → 01 comparison there will look better for 00h than it really is.

**On "redoes DFT on those structures":** I don't think a second DFT pass is needed. The frames we sample already get full production DFT, so the bad ones go straight into training. If you meant a cheap screening DFT first and then full DFT on the bad frames, it can't work at this accuracy. In the A0b tests, Γ-only DFT differs from the converged mesh by 30–106 meV/atom and 0.16–0.53 eV/Å. 00h's errors are about 4.5 meV/atom and 0.2 eV/Å, so the screen's own error would hide which structures are bad.

**Decision for you: DFT cost.** Iteration 01 samples 3 frames from each of 425 MD runs, which is about 1275 DFT frames, some of them 100–176 atoms. That is a large DFT array. I can cut it to 1–2 frames per run, or cap the total with a global FPS selection, before staging the DFT. Which do you want?

The MD array 7906537 is still waiting in the queue. The loop procedure is written up in `DP/README.md` and §6 of `results_Fe/FE_DEEPMD_SUMMARY.md`.

DFT: PBEsol (GGA=PS), Fe_pv, ENCUT 800, Γ-centred 2×2×2, SIGMA = k_BT per band. Not mixable with our PBE/Fe_sv data; Fe_pv PAW spheres overlap at 330 GPa.

Split (RC 11-19 "My lammps and deepmd and plumed installations work"): dp train/test/compress, LAMMPS, PLUMED → RC's deepmd_py311 (v3.2.0; no dpdata/asaplib there); only the mldp data scripts and asap → Xin's env. Don't pip-install into deepmd_py311.

### Claude (11-23 04:56)

Understood on the DFT. Nothing does a second pass on the same structures: each sampled frame gets DFT once.

**Your workflow.** Xin's mldp workflow does most of the loop, and our tools follow it:
- FPS selects a fixed number of frames per trajectory: her `select_frames.py -n`, our `fe_dp_sample.py --nsel`. That number sets the DFT count.
- `analysis.py` compares the model with DFT, and frames inside the error cutoffs go into training. Our `fe_dp_split.py` does the same, with the cutoffs set so that 10–20 % of frames qualify, as you asked on 11-20.

Her README has no step that chooses test structures and none that stops when the accuracy stops changing. The two small tools I added this morning, `fe_dp_testset.py` and `fe_dp_accuracy.py`, only fill those two steps.

I've kept 3 frames per MD run, which means about 1275 DFT frames for iteration 01. If you want a smaller array, tell me the number per run.

**Does MPI speed it up?** Only with one MPI rank per GPU. Putting several ranks on one GPU makes it slower. I measured this on P100s with 00h (job 7908389):

| cell | 1 rank, 1 GPU | 2 ranks, 1 GPU | 4 ranks, 1 GPU | 2 ranks, 2 GPUs | 4 ranks, 2 GPUs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| edge dipole, 176 atoms (steps/s) | 78 | 44 | 25 | 96 | — |
| hcp, 4096 atoms (steps/s) | 6.4 | 5.6 | 5.1 | **11.8** | 9.9 |

Four independent 64-atom runs sharing one GPU total 95 steps/s, against 103 for one run alone, so sharing a GPU gains nothing.

- **Small exploration cells:** one GPU per array task, as now, is already the best arrangement.
- **4096-atom Fe anelastic runs:** two GPUs with one rank each nearly doubles the speed (1.84×). The new model is slow at this size: 1 ns takes about 43 h on one P100, or 24 h on two. MgO with its simpler model ran 22.8 steps/s at 4096 atoms.

**A 28-core Broadwell node:** I don't think it would help.
- **DeePMD MD and training** run on the GPU, so a CPU-only node can't speed them up.
- **VASP:** one 28-core node is less than half of a single one of our 2 × 32-rank DFT jobs.
- **The queue is working:**
  - P100 jobs yesterday started within about 30 s, all 10 dislocation reruns at once.
  - Today's debug jobs started immediately.
  - The R1/R1b/R1d DFT arrays all got through.
  - The iteration-01 MD array (7906537) has been waiting about 25 min.

The one thing that would help is access to more GPUs, for the large Fe cells.

The MPI table is in §5 of `results_Fe/FE_DEEPMD_SUMMARY.md` and in `DP/01/speedtest/mpi/README.md`.

### Claude (11-23 04:58)

Yes, a dedicated GPU node would help, but as an addition to the queue rather than a replacement. How much depends on which GPU it has and how many.

**The queue works, but often slowly.** My 705 GPU jobs since 10-01:
- The median wait was 5 min.
- 35 % of jobs (249) waited more than 1 h, and 10 % waited more than 4.7 h. The worst wait was 36 h.
- The iteration-01 MD array (7906537) has been pending about 45 min so far.

The cost is less in GPU time than in waiting between the steps of the loop.

**One GPU roughly matches our average use.**
- We used 1629 GPU-hours since 10-01, which averages 30 GPU-h/day. One GPU running nonstop gives 24 GPU-h/day.
- On days we actually ran GPU jobs, use averaged 78 GPU-h, with a peak of 300 GPU-h on 10-07.
- So a dedicated node would carry the steady work: tests, retraining (16 h per model now) and long single runs. The 17-task exploration arrays would still go through the queue.

**What would make it most useful:**
1. **Two or more GPUs.** One MPI rank per GPU on two GPUs gave 1.84× at 4096 atoms (6.4 → 11.8 steps/s). That would bring a 1-ns Fe anelastic run from 43 h to about 24 h.
2. **The GPU model.** Our speeds are all for the P100. A V100 or newer should be faster, but our DeePMD GPU build is compiled for the P100 only (`build_gpu`, sm_60), so I would need to rebuild it for a different card. I have not measured any other card.
3. **The Broadwell CPU doesn't matter.** These runs are limited by the GPU: the 176-atom run gave 78 steps/s with 2 threads and 79 with 9.

Which GPU and how many does the node have? With that I can estimate the gain more exactly.

# SPDX-License-Identifier: LGPL-3.0-or-later
r"""Compact and Compressible degree-wise DPA4 descriptor.

DPA4C is the compact and compressible degree-wise member of the DPA4 family, a
graph-native local descriptor for lightweight training and for distillation
from DPA4. It reuses the DPA4 radial basis, bias-free radial network, type
embedding, and C³ cutoff envelope, and replaces equivariant message passing
with center-local moment reductions.

Degree :math:`\ell` retains :math:`C_\ell` channels from a profile derived
entirely from the scalar width, for :math:`2\le L\le 4`. Exact degree Grams
preserve the quadratic channel information, and low-rank Cartesian bispectrum
probes couple every non-scalar degree triple allowed by the O(3) triangle and
parity rules.

Evaluation is a single destination-local scan: one payload carries both
envelope masses and every degree-wise moment. The descriptor therefore
constructs no neighbor pairs, Wigner rotations, or source-node features, and
reduces the edge axis exactly once.
"""

### Claude (11-23 05:46)

No. 00h uses the TensorFlow backend with a hybrid `se_e2_a` + `se_e3` descriptor. When I was fixing the fcc/hcp error I tested only TF descriptors (`se_e2_a` variants, `se_e3` and DPA-1), and never checked which other descriptors our install has. DPA4C is in it, and I should have tried it.

**Why it fits our problem.** Our installed deepmd-kit is 3.2.0, and DPA4C's source documentation says:
- It keeps angular channels of degree ℓ up to 2–4, plus bispectrum terms that couple them. Model 00 failed because `se_e2_a` stops at ℓ = 1, where fcc and hcp sites look nearly the same. DPA4C carries the information that distinguished them.
- It is designed to be "compact and compressible", with one center-local pass and no neighbour-pair construction. Speed is now 00h's weak point: 6.4 steps/s at 4096 atoms on a P100, because of `se_e3`.

So it may fix the fcc/hcp energy and be faster as well. That is still to be measured.

**Two things stand in the way:**
1. **Backend.** DPA4C exists only in the PyTorch-export backend (`pt_expt`), not in TF. LAMMPS can load those models: the env has `libdeepmd_backend_ptexpt.so`.
2. **No GPU PyTorch.** The PyTorch in `deepmd_py311` is a CPU-only build (`torch.version.cuda` is None), so DPA4C could not be trained or run on a GPU there. Fixing that means installing a CUDA PyTorch. I won't pip-install into your `deepmd_py311` without your OK. I'd make a separate clone, e.g. `deepmd_py311_pt`, and leave yours untouched.

**Proposed test, the same one that picked out 00t3b:**
- Train DPA4C with fparam on the 300 K hcp/fcc training frames only, with the 00t3b settings.
- Pass mark: perfect-crystal E(fcc) − E(hcp) near the DFT 122.6 meV/atom, and errors per pressure–temperature state of about 5 meV/atom.
- Then measure LAMMPS speed at 176 and 4096 atoms against 00h.

That needs a few P100-hours once the env exists. If DPA4C passes, iteration 02 would retrain with it in place of `se_e3`. The iteration-01 exploration with 00h can carry on regardless, since its DFT frames are useful to either model.

Shall I build the separate env and run the test?

### Claude (11-23 05:48)

I checked this directly, and DPA4C is not available through the TensorFlow backend in our install (deepmd-kit 3.2.0 in `deepmd_py311`). This is measured, not inferred:

1. **TF rejects it.** A 2-step `dp --tf train` with `"descriptor": {"type": "dpa4c"}` stops with `RuntimeError: Unknown descriptor type: dpa4c. Did you mean: dpa1?`
2. **Only two places register it.** `dpa4c` is registered in `deepmd/dpmodel/descriptor/dpa4c.py` and `deepmd/pt_expt/descriptor/dpa4c.py`. Nothing under `deepmd/tf/` mentions it. `deepmd/tf2/` has DPA1–DPA4 but not DPA4C.
3. **The source tree agrees.** In `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/deepmd-kit` the commit that added it is `bdb40072 feat(pt-expt): add compact descriptor DPA4C (#5972)`. Its compiled GPU kernels (`dpa4c_graph_compress*.cu`) are under `source/op/pt/`, the PyTorch side.

So the files you probably saw are the PyTorch-export (`--pt-expt`) and pure-Python (`dpmodel`) versions. Those don't work as installed either. The same tiny test with `dp --pt-expt train` crashes on import: `PackageNotFoundError: No package metadata was found for mpich`, raised in `deepmd/pt/cxx_op.py`. On top of that, the env's PyTorch is a CPU-only build (`torch.version.cuda` is None), so even with the import fixed it could not train on a GPU.

To use DPA4C we'd need a PyTorch environment that works on the GPU. I'd build it as a separate clone so `deepmd_py311` stays as it is, unless you'd rather fix `deepmd_py311` itself. Then I'd run the same quick fcc−hcp descriptor test that picked 00t3b. If you have a working DPA4C setup somewhere else, point me to it and I'll use that instead.

### Claude (11-23 05:49)

You're right that the build is TensorFlow-only, and I didn't change that. But that is exactly why DPA4C isn't available to us: deepmd-kit has no TensorFlow version of DPA4C, only a PyTorch one.

**The build is still TF-only, as you made it:**
- Your `source/build` and the `source/build_gpu` I made on 10-06 have the same backend settings: `ENABLE_TENSORFLOW=ON`, `ENABLE_PYTORCH=OFF`, `ENABLE_JAX=OFF`, `ENABLE_PADDLE=OFF`.
- On 10-06 I only rebuilt the TF/LAMMPS side against the pip CUDA TensorFlow, to get the GPU working.

**Where the non-TF files came from (not from me):**
- The PyTorch backend libraries (`libdeepmd_backend_pt.so`, `libdeepmd_backend_ptexpt.so`) and the CPU-only PyTorch were installed on 09-28. That was the `conda create … deepmd-kit` that made the env, and the conda-forge package ships every backend.
- The Python `deepmd` package was reinstalled with pip on 10-06 at 09:20 from your source tree. That tree's newest commit is dated 08-19, so it includes DPA4C. My session logs have no `pip install` of deepmd, so I don't think I did that reinstall.

**DPA4C was written for PyTorch only:**
- The commit that added it is "feat(pt-expt): add compact descriptor DPA4C" (`bdb40072`, 08-18).
- Its GPU kernels are in `source/op/pt/`.
- There is no DPA4C code anywhere under `deepmd/tf/`.

That fits the test: `dp --tf train` with `dpa4c` fails with "Unknown descriptor type: dpa4c".

So to try DPA4C we would need a PyTorch build of deepmd-kit with GPU support. The 00h model and the running iteration-01 MD stay on TF either way. Do you want me to set up a separate PyTorch environment for a DPA4C test, or stay with the TF hybrid descriptor?

def load_mpi_library() -> None:
    """Load MPI library.

    When building with cibuildwheel, the link to the MPI library is lost
    after the wheel is repaired.
    """
    if platform.system() == "Linux":
        libname = "libmpi.so.*"
    elif platform.system() == "Darwin":
        libname = "libmpi.*.dylib"
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("Unsupported platform")
    MPI_LIB = next(p for p in metadata.files("mpich") if p.match(libname)).locate()
    # use CDLL to load the library
    CDLL(MPI_LIB, mode=RTLD_GLOBAL)


if GLOBAL_CONFIG.get("cibuildwheel", "0") == "1" and platform.system() in (
    "Linux",

):

### Claude (11-23 06:43)

The PyTorch build hasn't started yet. The 17 iteration-01 MD jobs are still running with this environment, and swapping its libraries now could break the runs they start later. They should finish within about 40 minutes. I'll start the build automatically when they do.

**Plan**
1. **Backups (done).** The current deepmd libraries, the LAMMPS deepmd plugin, the CPU-only PyTorch, and `pip freeze` / `conda list` are saved in `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/anaconda2/deepmd_py311_backup_2026-11-23_pytorch`.
2. **GPU PyTorch.** Install PyTorch 2.11.0 for CUDA 12.6, which matches the version the installed DeePMD Python package was built against. I'll install it without its own NVIDIA libraries so it uses the CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.27 set your TensorFlow already uses. Only the libraries TensorFlow doesn't have get added: NCCL, cuSPARSELt, NVSHMEM, CUPTI, cuFile, NVTX and Triton.
3. **Fix the PyTorch-side import error.** DeePMD's PyTorch backend currently crashes on import (the missing `mpich` package metadata). The fix is a one-line config change, and I'll back up the file first.
4. **Rebuild the DeePMD C++ libraries** in your source tree (`source/build_gpu`) with both TensorFlow and PyTorch on, compiled for every GPU type here: P100, V100, A100, L40S, H100/H200, B300 (sm 60, 70, 80, 89, 90, 100, 103).
   - LAMMPS and PLUMED are not rebuilt. Your `lmp` loads DeePMD through `libdeepmd_c`, which picks the TensorFlow or PyTorch plugin at run time.
5. **Checks before releasing the env.**
   - TensorFlow: the 00h speed test must still give about 78 steps/s on the 176-atom edge-dipole cell.
   - PLUMED: a LAMMPS run with `fix plumed`.
   - PyTorch: a small DPA4C training on a P100, then a LAMMPS run of the resulting model.

**One limit on "all GPUs": the PyTorch builds can't cover both the P100 and the B300.**
- The CUDA 12.6 PyTorch has kernels for sm 50–90 only, with no portable fallback code, so PyTorch models won't run on the B300.
- PyTorch builds for CUDA 12.8 and later support the B300 but drop the P100.
- Our own DeePMD GPU code will cover all of them. TensorFlow already covers all of them: kernels for sm 60–90, plus portable code that recompiles for the B300.

I chose the CUDA 12.6 PyTorch because your work runs on P100s. Covering the B300 too would mean compiling PyTorch from source, which is a multi-hour build; say if you want that.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J dpbuildPT
#SBATCH --nodes 1
#SBATCH --ntasks 1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 32
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=3GB
#SBATCH -q debug
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH -o slurm-%j.out
# deepmd-kit C++ (TF + PyTorch, sm_60 + sm_90) configure + make on a compute node (the login node is overloaded).
# Rerun to continue make; does NOT install (make install is a separate step after checks).
ROOT=$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
[ -f $ROOT/Makefile ] || $ROOT/configure_gpu.sh > $ROOT/configure_pt.log 2>&1 || { echo configure failed; tail -30 $ROOT/configure_pt.log; exit 1; }
grep -E "PyTorch|Torch|CUDA|ABI|Build files" $ROOT/configure_pt.log | grep -v "^  " | head -20
timeout 1500 $ROOT/make_gpu.sh > $ROOT/make_pt.log 2>&1; rc=$?
echo "make rc=$rc"; grep -E "error|Error" $ROOT/make_pt.log | head -20; tail -3 $ROOT/make_pt.log | cut -c1-200
EOF
sed -i 's/make -j16/make -j32/' $B/make_gpu.sh; chmod +x $B/build_job.sh; cd $B && rm -rf CMakeCache.txt CMakeFiles Makefile && sbatch build_job.sh

# deepmd.kernels.cuda.*.op_available). The CUDA language is scoped per
# directory, so it must be enabled here: the sibling GPU library turns it on
# only within its own subtree, which does not cover this target.
if(USE_CUDA_TOOLKIT AND DEEPMD_TORCH_HAS_CUDA)
  find_package(CUDAToolkit REQUIRED)
  option(DEEPMD_ENABLE_DPA1_HIGH_LMAX
         "Instantiate experimental DPA1 CUDA kernels for lmax greater than one"
         OFF)
  if(NOT DEFINED CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES)
    # CUDA 12.9 CCCL fails to compile CUB/Thrust with -arch=all.
    if(CUDAToolkit_VERSION VERSION_GREATER_EQUAL "12.9" AND CUDAToolkit_VERSION
                                                            VERSION_LESS "13.0")
      set(CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES all-major)

### Claude (11-23 09:01)

The PyTorch build is working and is now in its last rebuild. I should have reported sooner; here is where it stands.

**What works so far (tested on GPU nodes):**
- **TensorFlow 00h in LAMMPS still works on the P100:** 80 steps/s on the 176-atom cell, against 78 before the change.
- **Your PLUMED is the one in use.** LAMMPS loads your PLUMED 2.9.2 build ("compiled on Sep 30"), byte-identical to `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/plumed-2.9.2`. `fix plumed` ran and wrote COLVAR. I did not recompile PLUMED or LAMMPS, and neither needs it.
- **GPU PyTorch is installed in `deepmd_py311`:** 2.11.0+cu126, sharing TensorFlow's CUDA 12.9 and cuDNN libraries, which are unchanged. The DeePMD C++ libraries were rebuilt with TF + PyTorch, and LAMMPS picks the backend at run time.
- **DPA4C runs end to end on a V100:** training (3000 steps, 4 min), freezing to `.pt2`, and LAMMPS MD with that model at 244 steps/s on the 176-atom cell. The model is barely trained, so that number shows the code path works, not the final speed.

**Two problems I found and fixed:**
1. **The first build left out sm_60.** PyTorch's build system replaces the requested GPU list with its own, and that list excludes the P100. Installing it would have broken your P100 TensorFlow runs. I now force the list with `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST`.
2. **Warp was the CPU-only conda build.** Warp is used by DeePMD's PyTorch neighbour lists. I replaced it with the CUDA build from PyPI, and the old copy is backed up.

**One limit: DPA4C cannot run on the P100 at all.** Both training and the LAMMPS `.pt2` model are compiled with Triton, which needs compute capability 7.0 or higher; the P100 is 6.0. The error is "GPUTooOldForTriton". That is why I'm adding the V100 (sm_70) to the build. It costs the same 10 units/h as the P100 and, as you say, has short queues. So the build now targets P100 + V100 + H200 and is compiling (job 7932814).

**Next, about 30 min:**
1. Install the rebuilt libraries.
2. Run one check job on the P100 and one on the V100: TF 00h + PLUMED in LAMMPS, GPU PyTorch and Warp, `dp test` on DPA4C, and LAMMPS with DPA4C.
3. Report the results.

Your TF 00h workflow is unaffected throughout. Backups of everything I replaced are in `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/anaconda2/deepmd_py311_backup_2026-11-23_pytorch`.

Separately, the iteration-01 MD with 00h finished: 424 of 425 runs ran to completion. The edge dipole at 350 GPa, 6700 K (1.05 T_m, above melting) lost an atom and stopped.

### Claude (11-23 09:11)

The PyTorch build is finished, and both GPU-node checks passed on everything except DPA4C on the P100, which can't run it.

| check (176-atom Fe cell, LAMMPS) | P100 | V100 |
|---|---|---|
| TF 00h model + your PLUMED 2.9.2 | 79.5 steps/s, COLVAR written | **130 steps/s**, COLVAR written |
| GPU PyTorch and Warp | ok | ok |
| DPA4C train, freeze, `dp test` | fails | ok (E 2.3 meV/atom, F 0.15 eV/Å on its own training frames) |
| DPA4C model in LAMMPS | fails | 248 steps/s (toy model, 3000 training steps) |

- **Your PLUMED is the one in use.** LAMMPS loads your 2.9.2 library ("compiled on Sep 30"), which is byte-identical to `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/plumed-2.9.2`. I did not recompile PLUMED or LAMMPS; only the DeePMD libraries changed.
- **Why DPA4C fails on the P100.** DPA4C training and its LAMMPS model are compiled by Triton, which needs a GPU of compute capability 7.0 or newer; the P100 is 6.0. So I built for P100, V100 and H200.
- **The V100 is the better buy for TF runs too.** At the same 10 units/h, 00h runs 1.6× faster than on the P100 (130 against 79.5 steps/s). Given the short V100 queues, I suggest moving production DeePMD runs to V100s.
- **What changed in `deepmd_py311`:**
  - GPU PyTorch 2.11.0+cu126 now sits alongside TensorFlow's CUDA libraries, which are unchanged.
  - The CPU-only conda Warp was replaced by the CUDA build.
  - I edited one line in DeePMD's `run_config.ini` to fix the import crash.
  - The C++ libraries were rebuilt from your source tree for sm 60/70/90.

  Everything I replaced is backed up in `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/anaconda2/deepmd_py311_backup_2026-11-23_pytorch`. Results are in `DP/envtest_pt/README.md`.
- **Warning about conda.** Conda still believes its own PLUMED 2.10.2 is installed, so a future `conda install` or update in this env could overwrite your PLUMED library again. Its copies are the `*.bak` files in `lib/`.

**Xin's trajectory test.** I couldn't find the paper or its SI: `Anelasticity/Papers` has nothing newer than Oct 15, and nothing matches "2025GL119400" or "Phase Relations". Where did you put them?

Here is how I'd add his test to the loop as a final check:
- After each retraining, run a short LAMMPS trajectory of a small cell (64–100 atoms) with the model at a few P–T states.
- Run DFT on every 5–10 steps.
- Compare energy, and also forces and stress, which come free with each DFT run.

Unlike our test sets, these frames are neither chosen by the model's errors nor by FPS, so they are unbiased. That makes them the right numbers for the "total accuracy stops changing" criterion. Consecutive frames are strongly correlated, so I would quote errors per trajectory rather than per frame.

**Your call: a DPA4C test on a V100?** It would be the same fcc−hcp test that picked 00t3b: train on the 300 K hcp/fcc data and compare fcc−hcp with DFT's 122.6 meV/atom. If you agree, I'll run it at a cost of a few V100-hours. Iteration 01 carries on either way; its MD finished with 424 of 425 runs complete, and the next step is selecting frames for DFT.

### Claude (11-23 09:18)

I found both papers on the second look, and I've started the DPA4C training on V100s. Before the next DFT step I need a decision from you on how many frames to run, because the large defect cells make it very expensive. Earlier I listed only files with recent dates, and these two kept their September dates when copied, so I missed them.

**What Xin's paper does to validate the potential (GRL 2026, §2.5 and SI Figs. S3–S4):**
1. **Held-out test set:** 12,543 configurations not used in training, up to 8000 K and ~400 GPa. Errors are 5.13 meV/atom (energy), 0.296 eV/Å (forces) and 0.587 GPa (stress).
2. **Trajectory test:** MD with the potential on 384-atom cells, larger than anything in the training set, for post-stishovite, seifertite and liquid at 120 GPa and 6000 K. DFT is then run on frames along each trajectory. Energy errors are 3.27, 2.27 and 5.21 meV/atom, the same as on the test set. The paper compares energies only; I'd add forces and stress, since each DFT run gives them anyway.
3. **How the training data were selected:** se_e2_a descriptor, structures sampled by enhanced-sampling MD in LAMMPS with PLUMED, then picked by PCA plus FPS. The final set is 7,709 configurations.

For Fe I'd add the trajectory test as the final check of each iteration. That means MD with the current model on a 64-atom cell at about three states, DFT every 5–10 steps, and errors reported per trajectory. I estimate about 1,500 core-h per iteration, but have not measured it.

**DPA4C on V100s: submitted, still waiting in the queue.**
- **00t4c (job 7934148):** quick descriptor test, 100k steps on the 300 K hcp/fcc data only, about 2 h. It's the same check that picked 00t3b: fcc − hcp should come out near the DFT 122.6 meV/atom, which tells us early whether DPA4C can separate the two.
- **00d (job 7934149):** the full model on all 670 frames of 00h's training data, 1M steps at ~0.05 s/step, so roughly 14 h.

Both jobs freeze the model when done, then compute fcc − hcp, run `dp test`, and compute the per-state errors (`dp_state_errors.py`) for comparison with 00h. Settings are DPA4C's recommended example values plus the temperature (fparam) input. Iteration 01's bad-frame selection will use 00d's errors, so the retraining continues with DPA4C.

**Decision for you: how many iteration-01 frames go to DFT.** The 00h MD finished: 424 of 425 runs. At 3 frames per run that is ~1,275 frames. My cost estimate is extrapolated from the existing defect frames on 2 × 32 cores; I have not measured the 128- and 176-atom cells:

| cells | frames | DFT time per frame | core-h |
|---|---|---|---|
| 52–72 atoms: hcp, fcc, vacancies, s7, stacking fault | ~675 | 200–700 s | ~4,000 |
| twin (100 atoms) | 150 | 4,800–11,200 s, measured | ~21,000 |
| dislocation dipoles (88–176 atoms) | ~450 | extrapolated | ~120,000 |

That totals about 145,000 core-h, and the dislocation and twin cells are almost all of it. I suggest:
- keep 3 frames per run for the small cells;
- take 1 frame per run for the twin and dislocation cells, which comes to about 50,000 core-h in total;
- or, cheaper still, sample the small cells in this iteration and leave the large cells for a later one.

Which do you want?

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fe DeePMD iteration loop, step 2: sample the exploration MD and stage the DFT (ANELASTICITY_PLAN_FE.md §3.2;
X. Deng's mldp steps 1-4: SOAP descriptors, farthest-point selection, extraction, recal dirs).

For every run of DP/NN/md/runs.txt (fe_dp_explore.py):
  - status from log.lammps (finished / unfinished / LAMMPS ERROR); frames are sampled from whatever was dumped, since
    the frames just before a failure are the worst-predicted ones;
  - frames of the first --skip ps dropped; frames with a pair closer than --dfrac * d_nn dropped as broken
    (the MD collapsed; DFT on them is wasted and often does not converge);
  - SOAP (r_cut 6, n_max 6, l_max 6, sigma 0.44, frame average, as soap_fps.py / asap) + FPS: --nsel frames per run;
  - staged as R1b/R1d: R1/<set>/<run>/deepmd (box.npy, coord.npy, type.raw, source.txt = MD step of each frame),
    R1/<set>/<run>/recal/<n>/ (POSCAR + INCAR, KPOINTS, POTCAR, n = 1, 2, ...; the recal_dpdata.py -rv no layout),
    R1/inputs/<set>_<run>/; R1/tasks_<set>.txt (for R1/fe_r1d_job.sh) and R1/bands_<set>.txt.
DFT settings: fe_r1_old.recal_incar (ENCUT 700, SIGMA = k_B T of the run, NBANDS rule); k-points: the true shifted
2x2x2 (A0c2) for the 62-64-atom hcp/fcc/vacancy cells, Monkhorst-Pack ceil(16 A / L) (fe_r1d_defects.kpoints_auto,
mean cell of the selected frames) for sf, s7, tw13.

usage (X. Deng's mambaforge python: ase, dscribe, scipy):
  fe_dp_sample.py DP/NN/md R1 --set itNN --potcar POTCAR [--nsel 3] [--skip 2] [--dfrac 0.6] [-j 4]
2026-11-21.

def smooth_even(x):
    n = int(np.ceil(x))
    while True:
        m = n
        for p in (2, 3, 5, 7):
            while m % p == 0:
                m //= p
        if m == 1 and n % 2 == 0:
            return n
        n += 1

                os.remove(os.path.join(d, f))
        inc = [l for l in open(os.path.join(d, 'INCAR')) if not l.split('=')[0].strip() in
               ('LREAL', 'AMIN', 'NGX', 'NGY', 'NGZ', 'NGXF', 'NGYF', 'NGZF')]
        inc += ['LREAL = Auto\n', 'AMIN = 0.01\n'] + [f'NG{x} = {n}\n' for x, n in zip('XYZ', ng)] + \
               [f'NG{x}F = {2 * n}\n' for x, n in zip('XYZ', ng)]
        open(os.path.join(d, 'INCAR'), 'w').write(''.join(inc))
        k, kp = kpoints_auto(cell)
        open(os.path.join(d, 'KPOINTS'), 'w').write(kp)
        tasks.append(os.path.relpath(d, a.r1))
        print(f'{os.path.relpath(d, a.r1):34} L {np.round(L, 2)} NG {ng} k {k}')
    with open(os.path.join(a.r1, f'tasks_{a.name}.txt'), 'w') as f:
        f.write(f'# {a.name} restaged with LREAL Auto, AMIN 0.01, NG* = {a.dens}/A, even k (fe_r1d_regrid.py)\n')
        f.write('\n'.join(tasks) + '\n')
    print(f'{len(tasks)} dirs -> tasks_{a.name}.txt')
if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

### Claude (11-23 09:44)

I've submitted the iteration-01 DFT array, using only cells of 100 atoms or fewer and no dislocations. The catch is the CPU queue: Slurm's estimated start for it is about Dec 6.

**What is set up:**
- **Frames selected.** From the 00h MD I took 3 frames per run, by the same structure-diversity (SOAP + FPS) selection as before. That gives 825 frames from 275 runs. The cells are hcp, fcc, one and two vacancies, the stacking fault, Σ7, the {10−12} twin, and the sheared versions of those runs. 168 collapsed frames were dropped.
- **Twin SCF fix applied.** The 150 twin frames got the settings that made the twin cells converge on 11-21: LREAL Auto, AMIN 0.01, the 9.6/Å FFT grid and even k-meshes.
- **DFT array 7936152, 825 tasks.** Each task runs on 2 × 32 cores with a 5 h limit. The longest twin frame so far took 3.1 h. The total should be about 25,000 core-h.
- **What happens after the DFT:**
  1. The DPA4C model 00d picks out the badly predicted frames, which go into training.
  2. The rest become the pool, and the test structures are selected from it.
  3. Retrain with DPA4C on a V100.
  4. Check whether the total test accuracy has stopped changing.
- **Dislocations later.** Once these cells are trained, I'll run DFT on about 50 dislocation frames, add the worst 5–10, retrain, and repeat. That follows your two messages, and I've written it into `R1/README.md` Part 6 and my notes.

**The CPU queue is the bottleneck.**
- The `expansion` partition is nearly full: 513 of 525 nodes allocated. Slurm's estimate for a 2-node job is Dec 6, about two weeks out, for every CPU type I tried.
- These estimates assume every running job uses its full time limit, so real starts usually come earlier through backfill. The R1 arrays got through in about a day.
- Many of the nodes are held by your own large `rn*`/`rnb*` arrays (job 7831563 alone has 17–39 nodes per task). If those can wait, this DFT will start sooner.
- I said earlier that a dedicated 28-core Broadwell node wouldn't help, and that's still my estimate. On its own it would need about 2–3 weeks for these 825 frames.

**DPA4C jobs:** 00t4c (7934148, the quick fcc − hcp test) and 00d (7934149, full training) are both still pending for V100s. They need no CPU nodes, so they don't depend on the DFT queue.

2. Key Technical Concepts

- **Model 00h (TF, se_e2_a+se_e3 hybrid):**
  - fcc−hcp 124.5 meV/atom (DFT 122.6; model 00 gave 53.8).
  - State-mean errors: rms 4.5 meV/atom at σ < 0.07 eV; groups 1.7–7.1; worst +17.7 (fcc P100 T2800).
  - F 0.198 eV/Å (4.9 % of the rms DFT force component of 4.08); stress 0.67 GPa.
  - These are training-set errors only (no validation set).
- **MD speed:**
  - P100: 00h at 79–103 steps/s for 64–176 atoms; 4096 atoms 6.4 steps/s on one P100, 11.8 on two P100s with one rank each. More than one rank per GPU is slower.
  - V100: 00h at 130 steps/s on 176 atoms (P100: 79.5).
- **Iteration loop:**
  - fe_dp_split: the worst 15 % per T band go to training, the rest to the pool.
  - fe_dp_testset: SOAP-FPS of 30 % per system type → DP/test/itNN.
  - fe_dp_accuracy: RMSE E/F/S for the previous vs new model on all test structures. Converged when ΔE < 0.5 meV/atom, ΔF < 5 %, ΔS < 0.1 GPa.
  - Selection bias: the newest test set flatters the previous model, so convergence uses the earlier sets from it02 on.
- **Xin's validation (GRL 2026, §2.5, SI Figs. S3–S4):**
  - 12,543 held-out configurations: RMSE 5.13 meV/atom, 0.296 eV/Å, 0.587 GPa.
  - MD of 384-atom cells at 120 GPa / 6000 K, larger than training, with DFT along the trajectory: energy RMSE 2.27–5.21 meV/atom.
  - Training: se_e2_a; LAMMPS+PLUMED enhanced sampling; PCA+FPS; 7,709 configurations.
- **DPA4C:**
  - Exists only in the pt_expt backend (commit bdb40072 "feat(pt-expt)…"); TF reports "Unknown descriptor type: dpa4c".
  - Training of graph-lower models always uses torch.compile/Inductor, so it needs Triton, which needs compute capability ≥ 7.0. It fails on the P100 (GPUTooOldForTriton) and works on the V100.
  - Frozen .pt2 (AOTInductor); LAMMPS needs `atom_modify map yes`.
  - Water example settings: channels 32, lmax 2, rcut 6, bessel n_radial 16, radial_modes 4, float32, fitting 192×3 silu, wsd lr, HybridMuon, MAE loss pe = pf = 20, pv = 5.
  - V100: 0.046 s/batch.
- **Env build facts:**
  - pip torch 2.11.0+cu126 (matches the PyPI deepmd-kit 3.2.0 wheel built with torch 2.11) installed --no-deps, using TF's nvidia CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.27 pip libs.

### Claude (11-23 11:23)

The job that finished was **00t4c (job 7934148)**, the quick check of DPA4C before the full training. It trains on only the ten 300 K hcp/fcc states, for 100k steps. Earlier, the standard descriptor alone failed this same test. It found fcc and hcp nearly equal in energy, even though DFT puts fcc 122.6 meV/atom higher. Adding the 3-body term fixed that. This run asked whether DPA4C also gets it right before we commit to it. It ran 72 min on a V100, about 12 compute units.

**It passes:**

| model | descriptor | E(fcc) − E(hcp), meV/atom (DFT 122.6) | 300 K state energy errors fcc / hcp, meV/atom | force rmse fcc / hcp, eV/Å |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 00t | standard (se_e2_a) | 0.2 | 47 / 71 | 0.178 / 0.292 |
| 00t3b | standard + 3-body (se_e2_a + se_e3) | 124.4 | 5.3 / 5.8 | 0.148 / 0.176 |
| 00t4c | DPA4C | 127.0 | 0.3 / 0.6 | 0.057 / 0.046 |

- **Fitting:** DPA4C fits the 300 K data about 10 times better in energy and about 3 times better in forces than the 3-body model on the same data. Overall the energy error is 0.86 meV/atom and the force error 0.053 eV/Å.
- **fcc − hcp:** DPA4C is 4.4 meV/atom above DFT, against 1.8 for the 3-body model, so on this one number it is a little worse. Those perfect cells are not in the training data.
- **Caveat:** all of these are errors on the training frames. There was no held-out set in this test. The held-out comparison comes from the iteration test sets.

**00d (job 7934149)**, the full DPA4C training on all the 00h data, is running normally:
- It is at step 130k of 1M after 85 min, with an estimated finish around **20:40 tonight**. That is well inside its 36 h limit, so no restart should be needed.
- When it finishes, the job itself reports fcc − hcp, the per-state errors and the overall errors. I'll compare those with 00h: fcc − hcp 124.5, state errors 4.5 meV/atom, forces 0.198 eV/Å.
- 00d then becomes the model that selects the iteration-01 frames, once the DFT array (7936152) runs.

I've added the result to the 00t4c README in the run directory and to the summary table in `results_Fe/FE_DEEPMD_SUMMARY.md`, and updated INPROGRESS.
